definition: A named block of code that performs a job. Source: Official Python vocabulary (Python tutorial).
A higher-level unit of software with an interface and an implementation. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 4 (to verify against book).

Something that assigns an input to a category. In this course it proposes a business category from website evidence. Source: Standard data and machine-learning vocabulary, specialised for this course.
A score used here to show how strongly the model supports a suggestion. Source: Course domain term; its exact meaning must be defined by the chosen model.
The short, plain list of about ten business categories the Company Enricher can suggest, such as Retail, Manufacturing, or Software & IT. Source: Course domain term, defined in the practice project.
A proposed business category that still carries evidence and review status. Source: Domain language for this course.
Where a value is in a sequence of work, such as candidate, verified, or classified. Source: Course-authored teaching word.
The real business problem the software works on. Source: Standard software vocabulary; important in Domain-Driven Design.
The point where this code meets another system or responsibility. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Words agreed and used by one domain's experts and developers. Source: Eric Evans's Domain-Driven Design term, Chapter 2 (to verify against book); not universal software vocabulary.
Text inside a function that explains how to use it. Source: Official Python vocabulary (PEP 257).
Python's built-in marker for "no value here." Source: Official Python vocabulary (Python documentation).
What other code must know to use a function or module. Source: Standard software vocabulary; central in Ousterhout Chapter 4 (to verify against book).
The steps currently used to do the work. Source: Standard software vocabulary; central in Ousterhout Chapter 4 (to verify against book).
An outside change, such as saving data or sending a message. Source: Standard software vocabulary; PEP 257 says function documentation should describe side effects.

A unit of code with an interface and an implementation. It can be a function, class, subsystem, or service. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 4 (to verify against book).
A simplified view of something that leaves out unimportant details. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 4 (to verify against book).
Any data a function uses to produce its result, whether passed in or read from elsewhere. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
The value a function gives back to its caller. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
Something outside the function that it relies on, such as a website, file, database, or clock. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
An external dependency that does not appear in the function's parameters. Source: Course-authored teaching term.

Something you must know to change code safely, with no sign in the code that you need to know it. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 2 (to verify against book).

The same design knowledge appearing in more than one module, so a change to it touches all of them. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 5 (to verify against book).

Anything about the structure of a system that makes it hard to understand and modify. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 2 (to verify against book).
A simple change requiring edits in many different places. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 2 (to verify against book).
How much a developer needs to know to complete a task. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 2 (to verify against book).
Code that cannot be understood or modified in isolation from other code. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 2 (to verify against book).
Facts a reader needs to know that the code does not show. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 2 (to verify against book).

A small, visible sign of neglect that, left unfixed, encourages more neglect. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 3, "Software Entropy" (to verify against book).
A module that provides powerful functionality behind a simple interface. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 4 (to verify against book).

A module whose interface is complicated compared with the functionality it provides. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 4 (to verify against book).
A method that does little except pass its arguments to another method. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 7 (to verify against book).
A Python attribute whose value is computed by a method each time it is read. Source: Official Python vocabulary (built-in functions: property).

A module whose functionality meets today's needs while its interface is general enough for several uses. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 6, checked in the author's free extract.

Each piece of knowledge in a system should be expressed in exactly one authoritative place. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 9, "DRY - The Evils of Duplication", checked in the publisher's free excerpt.

Two parts are orthogonal when a change to one does not affect the other. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 10, "Orthogonality" (to verify against book).
The same fact or rule needed in more than one place, even if the code text differs. Source: Course-authored plain definition, following The Pragmatic Programmer's DRY topic.

Knowledge two pieces of code must both have, which is a reason to keep them together. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 9 (to verify against book).
A Python mapping from keys to values, such as category to hit count. Source: Official Python vocabulary (Python tutorial: dictionaries).
Considering two or more substantially different designs before choosing one. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 11 (to verify against book).

A thin, working path through every layer of a system, kept and filled in over time. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 12, "Tracer Bullets" (to verify against book).

A throwaway experiment built to answer one specific question. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 13, "Prototypes and Post-it Notes" (to verify against book).
A value that always comes back from an operation and describes what happened. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
A field on a result that says which outcome happened, such as accepted or needs review. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
A Python object that signals an error and interrupts normal flow until something handles it. Source: Official Python vocabulary (tutorial: errors and exceptions).

Handling an exceptional condition at a low level so higher levels never see it. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 10 (to verify against book).
Handling many exceptions with one piece of code instead of many. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 10 (to verify against book).

Stopping as soon as the code finds an impossible state, instead of continuing with bad data. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 24, "Dead Programs Tell No Lies" (to verify against book).
Why a result needs a person: weak evidence or no website. Source: Course domain term.
Code that runs other code and checks one expected behaviour. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
A pytest function that prepares something tests need and passes it to them by name. Source: Official pytest vocabulary (fixtures).
One test function run once for each set of arguments. Source: Official pytest vocabulary (parametrize).
A test that pins what the code does today, so a change that alters it fails. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.

A test that checks a rule holds for many generated inputs. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 42, "Property-Based Testing" (to verify against book).
Giving the same result every time it runs with the same inputs. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
Something the code relies on that is likely to change or fail, such as a network service or the clock. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
Code at a boundary that translates between an outside system and the rest of the service. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A Python type that lists the methods an object must have, without requiring inheritance. Source: Official Python vocabulary (typing.Protocol).
Passing a dependency in from outside instead of creating or finding it inside. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A limit on how long to wait for an answer before giving up. Source: Official Python vocabulary (urllib.request.urlopen).

Restructuring existing code without changing its external behaviour. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 40, "Refactoring" (to verify against book).
A saved snapshot of changes in Git, with a message explaining them. Source: Official Git vocabulary (git-commit).
A new commit that undoes the changes of an earlier commit. Source: Official Git vocabulary (git-revert).

A system that records every change to files so any earlier state can be recovered. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 19, "Version Control" (to verify against book).
A person who knows the business area well, such as a reviewer who categorises companies. Source: Standard DDD vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Working through examples with domain experts to distil a useful model. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 1 (to verify against book).
A concrete example of a situation and what should happen in it. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
A Python type with a fixed set of named values, such as Outcome.SUGGESTED. Source: Official Python vocabulary (enum).
An object defined by its identity and continuity over time, not by its attributes. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 5 (to verify against book).
An object that describes something, has no identity of its own, and is usually immutable. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 5 (to verify against book).
An operation in the model that does not belong naturally to any entity or value object. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 5 (to verify against book).
Unable to change after it is created. Source: Standard software vocabulary; Python's frozen dataclasses provide it.
What makes an entity the same one over time; here, company_id. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
A rule that must always be true, such as "confidence is between 0 and 1". Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
The explicit boundary within which one model and its language apply. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 14 (to verify against book).
A description of the bounded contexts in play and how they relate. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 14 (to verify against book).
A layer that translates between your model and another system's, keeping the other model out. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 14 (to verify against book).
The category a partner directory suggests for a company, translated into our categories. Source: Course domain term.
An explicit mapping from another system's values to yours. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
The most valuable and specialised part of the model, where design effort should go first. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 15 (to verify against book).
A part the system needs that is not special to this business. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 15 (to verify against book).
A part specific to this business that exists to support the core. Source: Standard DDD vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A short description of the core domain and the value it brings. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 15 (to verify against book).
Core code separated from supporting code so it can be understood alone. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 15 (to verify against book).
A small interface in the core that says what it needs from the outside world. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A requirement about how well a system works, such as speed or accuracy, rather than what it does. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A measured value that shows how well a quality is met. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
The value an indicator must meet for the quality to count as good. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
Of the items the service labelled, the share it labelled correctly. Source: Standard data and machine-learning vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall; the 95th percentile is beaten by 95% of them. Source: Standard statistics vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Example inputs with the correct answer decided by a person, used to measure a system. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
A question the system repeatedly asks of its stored data. Source: Course-authored plain definition.
The declared structure of a database: tables, columns, and their types. Source: Standard database vocabulary; see SQLite: CREATE TABLE.
A database that stores rows in tables and is queried with SQL. Source: Standard database vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
The column or columns that uniquely identify each row in a table. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (CREATE TABLE).
A column whose values must match a key in another table. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (foreign keys).
Storing each record as a self-contained document, such as JSON. Source: Standard database vocabulary; see PostgreSQL: JSON types.

An object that gives the model query access to stored objects in the model's own language, hiding the database details. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; concept checked in Evans's free DDD Reference; chapter to verify against book.
A separate sorted structure that lets the database find rows by some columns without reading the whole table. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (CREATE INDEX).
The steps the database will take to answer a query. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN).
The part of the database that chooses a query plan. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (query planning).
Reading every row of a table to answer a query. Source: Standard database vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
An index on more than one column, used left to right. Source: Standard database vocabulary; see SQLite query planning.
Extra work each write must do, such as updating indexes. Source: Standard database vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
One numbered, ordered change to a database schema. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
An integer stored in a SQLite database file that applications may use as a version number. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (PRAGMA user_version).
The SQL command that changes an existing table, for example by adding a column. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (ALTER TABLE).
Making only additive changes first, and removing old structures in a later release. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A change that existing code keeps working with. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Giving the same result whether it runs once or many times. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A bug where the outcome depends on the timing of actions that happen at the same time. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A cluster of objects treated as one unit for changes, with a boundary inside which invariants must hold. Source: Paraphrased from Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, Chapter 6 (to verify against book).
An index that refuses two rows with the same value in its columns. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (CREATE INDEX).
A group of database changes that succeed or fail together. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (transactions).
How much one transaction can see of another's changes while both are running. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (isolation in SQLite).
How well you can understand what a running system is doing from the data it produces. Source: Paraphrased from OpenTelemetry: Observability primer.
A timestamped record of an event. Source: Paraphrased from OpenTelemetry: Signals.
A measurement captured and aggregated over time, such as a count of outcomes. Source: Paraphrased from OpenTelemetry: Signals.
An identifier shared by every record about one request, so they can be found together. Source: Standard observability vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Writing log events as named fields, such as JSON, instead of free text. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A rule that notifies a person when an indicator crosses a threshold. Source: Standard operations vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.

Values that control a program's behaviour and can change without changing its code. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 32, "Configuration" (to verify against book).
How easily a decision can be changed or undone later. Source: Paraphrased from Thomas and Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition, Topic 11, "Reversibility" (to verify against book).
A named value set outside a program that the program can read, such as ENRICHER_DB_PATH. Source: Official Python vocabulary (os.environ).
A setting that turns a piece of behaviour on or off without a code change. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Returning a system to its previous working state. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Running the tests automatically on every change. Source: Standard software vocabulary; see GitHub Actions documentation.
The small part of a program where most of its time is spent. Source: Paraphrased from John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed., Chapter 20 (to verify against book).
A repeatable measurement of how fast something runs. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A tool that measures how much time a program spends in each function. Source: Official Python vocabulary (The Python Profilers).
A store of earlier results, used to answer repeated requests without redoing the work. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
The time between asking for something and getting it. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
A failure that may succeed if the same request is tried again. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
Trying a failed operation again after waits that grow each time. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
An identifier that lets a system recognise a repeated request and apply it only once. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
An insert that does something else, such as nothing, when the row already exists. Source: Official SQLite vocabulary (UPSERT).
Running with reduced capability instead of stopping when a dependency fails. Source: Standard software vocabulary; this plain definition is course-authored.
